newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Italian tycoon drops in to his Sarajevo shop.
newsitem.headline: Italian tycoon drops in to his Sarajevo shop.

text.p: Italian tycoon Luciano Benetton visited Sarajevo on Tuesday to get a first hand look at one his shops which has brought fashion chic to a city battered by war and poverty.
Benetton said he had intended to attend the clothing shop's opening two years ago in wartime, when sandbags lined shop windows and NATO warplanes were bombing Serb gunners.
"I'm sorry I was not in a position to come before...I wanted to be here when this shop opened during the war but it wasn't possible," Benetton told reporters.
The Benetton clothing shop opened in September 1995 in the last months of the Bosnian war, just as the siege of Sarajevo began to ease amid a NATO bombing campaign.
The sandbags protecting the shop windows are gone and the city is now safe from lethal shelling attacks since a peace treaty was signed in December 1995.
He said opening the store during the conflict had been a "big risk" but he said it was done in part to show solidarity with Bosnia's plight.
"We were thinking at that point during the war that Sarajevo deserves to be part of the world."
Sarajevans cannot afford to buy much at the shop, even though the prices are slightly cheaper than Benetton stores elsewhere.

Bosnian bloodshed made its way into one of Benetton's controversial advertising campaigns in 1994, when the company published a photo of blood-stained clothes belonging to a dead Bosnian Croat soldier.

The photo, accompanied with an appeal for peace from the father of the dead soldier, won awards for drawing attention to the horrors of war but was criticised by others for exploiting one family's tragedy.
Asked about the photo, Benetton said: "The photo was received well in the world except by some in German television stations. They said it was propaganda."
